analysis.one_liner: Extends the enlarged Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that lower monthly insurance bills.
analysis.headline: Three days after introduction, the Senate blocked the bill from debate, failing 51-48 on a procedural vote that needed 60 yes votes, with every Democrat and both independents in favor and 48 of 55 Republicans opposed.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend, for three years through 2028, the temporarily larger health insurance subsidies (premium tax credits) that Congress created in 2021 and expanded in 2022 for people buying coverage on the Affordable Care Act marketplaces. It would keep two changes that are otherwise set to end after 2025: eliminating the income cap that cuts off anyone earning more than 400% of the federal poverty level, and lowering the share of their income enrollees must pay toward premiums. Under current law, people above that income cap lose eligibility entirely and everyone else's subsidies shrink starting in 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Households buying their own insurance through the ACA marketplaces. People above 400% of the poverty line (roughly four times the poverty income for their family size) would regain eligibility for any subsidy at all, and people below it would keep the larger credits and smaller premium bills they would otherwise lose in 2026. Health insurers also benefit because the subsidies are paid to them as premiums for marketplace plans.

how_it_helps.text: Restores eligibility for premium tax credits to taxpayers whose household income exceeds 400% of the federal poverty line through 2028; under current law that cap comes back after 2025 and cuts them off completely.

Keeps the lowered 'applicable percentage' — the share of income enrollees must contribute toward their premium — in place through 2028, and keeps that percentage from being adjusted upward for inflation, so subsidies stay larger across all income ranges.
Takes effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, bridging exactly the window in which the enhanced subsidies are otherwise scheduled to lapse.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. The bill is a bare three-year extension with no spending cuts or tax offsets, so the larger credits — including new subsidies reaching households above the 400%-of-poverty cap — would be added to the deficit.

drawbacks.text: The extension carries no offset: the bill text is solely the tax-credit extension, so the full cost of larger and broader subsidies would be added to the federal deficit.

Some of the money would go to households that are not poor: eliminating the 400%-of-poverty cap extends subsidies well up the income scale, which critics of the original enhancement singled out as aid to families who can afford coverage without help.
Because the credit formula pays down a share of whatever premium insurers charge, part of any future premium growth lands on the federal budget rather than pushing insurers to hold prices down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The help is real and immediate: without this extension, people above 400% of poverty lose all subsidy eligibility and every other marketplace enrollee's credit shrinks in 2026. The honest cost is fiscal — a three-year, unpaid-for extension that also sends some aid up the income scale — but the bill extends an existing, well-understood subsidy rather than creating a new entitlement. The main design criticism is the missing offset, not the mechanism.

outcome.mechanism: It failed a Senate procedural vote three days after introduction — 51-48, nine short of the 60 needed just to begin debate — leaving the enhanced subsidies to lapse after 2025 under current law.

narrative.text: Chuck Schumer introduced the bill on December 8, 2025 with no cosponsors; it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, and a motion to proceed plus a cloture motion were filed the next day.

On December 11, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 51-48. The motion needed 60 votes; all 45 Democrats and both independents voted yes, 4 of 55 Republicans joined them, and the other 48 Republicans voted no.

Under current law, the elimination of the 400% income cap and the lowered subsidy percentages expire after 2025, so the failure left the enhancements set to lapse and premiums to rise for marketplace enrollees starting in 2026.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 48 senators who voted no got the outcome they sought: no extension, with the enhanced credits expiring after 2025 and no new federal subsidy spending. Marketplace enrollees above 400% of poverty are set to lose eligibility entirely, and everyone else's subsidies shrink.

industries.note: Premium tax credits are paid to insurers as premiums for marketplace plans, so extending the enhanced credits keeps subsidized customers enrolled who might otherwise drop coverage when the enhancements lapse. On this bill the insurers' interest runs alongside enrollees' — they profit from the same affordability help people receive.
By expanding eligibility and increasing subsidy amounts, the bill keeps more patients insured and paying, reducing uncompensated care that hospitals otherwise absorb.

analysis.trajectory: With the enhanced credits scheduled to lapse after 2025 and the 60-vote threshold unmet, a standalone extension of this kind is unlikely to advance in this Congress; any revival would most likely come as part of a broader negotiation, and even a late deal would leave enrollees facing higher premiums for part of 2026.
